questions.question: Why does Go have multiple return values, and what's the convention?
questions.title: Multiple Return Values
questions.direct_answer: Go functions can return several values at once: the (value, error) pattern is the ecosystem-wide convention. Error is LAST; on failure, other values are zero. It replaced exceptions — the error is visible in the signature and checked at the call site.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why multiple returns instead of exceptions — the design argument: with (T, error), the failure is visible in the SIGNATURE — you can't call the function without acknowledging the error slot (the compiler enforces using or explicitly discarding it). Exceptions hide the failure path — any call might throw, and you need docs to know. Go's signature IS the documentation.

Beyond errors — the honest other uses: (key, found) lookups, (min, max) computations, (value, ok) type assertions — the comma-ok pattern everywhere. Multiple returns aren't just for errors; they're Go's only way to return a compound result, and the (T, error) convention is the most common specialization.

The naming convention: return values can be named in the signature — func f() (result int, err error) — which initializes them (zero), allows naked returns, and enables defer modification (the defer topic). Named returns are documentation too: func Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) — the names in the docs ARE the signature's.
